transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you here today?

Yeah, so… I’m here because of my work physical, basically. I’m an auto mechanic, and they have us do those checkups, and the doctor there said my weight was too low. He seemed more concerned about it than I was, honestly.

I mean, I know I’m lighter than I used to be, but from my point of view it hasn’t felt like some big problem. If anything, I feel lighter on my feet when I’m playing basketball, and at the garage I don’t feel as weighed down moving around, getting under cars, up and down, that kind of thing. So it kind of caught me off guard that he made it sound like I needed to come talk to someone. But that’s what brought me in.
Have you been trying to lose weight or change your eating habits on purpose, or has your lower weight been more of an accident?

I guess it’s not exactly an accident, no. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m doing some big “diet” thing, like counting everything out or whatever, but most days I do keep it pretty limited.

Usually I’ll just have coffee in the morning, because I’m up and out early and I don’t really feel like dealing with food before work. Then the shop gets busy, jobs run late, somebody’s waiting on parts, you know how it goes, and by the time I think about eating I’ll maybe have a small sandwich or half of whatever’s around. At home it’s kind of the same thing — the house is busy, there’s always stuff going on — so I feel better just sticking to my own simple rules and not making a whole production out of meals.

So… yeah, I suppose I have changed how I eat on purpose, but in my head it’s more like keeping things simple and manageable, not like I’m trying to make myself sick or anything.
Do you feel distressed or concerned about your eating habits or weight, or has anyone else expressed worry about it besides your doctor?

I mean… I’m not really distressed about it, no. That’s probably part of why this feels a little strange to me. I know people are worried — the work doctor, and my family has made comments here and there, like telling me I’m looking too thin or asking if I’m eating enough — but I guess I kind of feel like they’re making more out of it than it is.

Because from where I’m standing, I’m still doing my job. I still get up, go to the shop, work on cars all day, handle what needs handling at home, and I’m still playing basketball on weekends. It’s not like I’m lying around unable to function or missing work or anything like that. So when people act like it’s this big serious thing, I don’t know… I hear them, but it doesn’t really match how I see it day to day.

I guess I understand why they notice it, because I have lost weight, but I don’t feel as worried about it as everybody else seems to be.
Do you have a fear of gaining weight or a strong desire to be thinner, even though others might see you as too thin?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t love putting it that way, like “fear,” because that sounds dramatic. But if I’m being honest, if I get on the scale and it’s even up a pound, or my jeans feel a little tighter around the waist, it sticks in my head more than it probably should.

I start thinking, like, okay, am I getting soft again? Am I going to feel heavier crawling around at work, getting up from under a car, bending and moving all day? Or when I’m playing basketball, am I going to be slower, not as quick getting up and down the court? That’s the kind of thing that bothers me.

So I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there wanting to look skinny exactly. It’s more that gaining weight feels like losing that lighter, quicker feeling, and I really don’t like that. Even if other people are saying I’m already too thin, in my head I’m thinking I don’t want it going the other direction.
Do you ever push yourself to exercise more or eat even less if you feel like you've eaten too much or gained a little weight?

I don’t know if I’d say I “push” myself exactly. It’s more like… if I feel like I’ve had too much, or things feel a little out of hand, I just tighten things back up. Like the next day I’ll keep it simple again — coffee in the morning, maybe a small sandwich later if I get a chance, or half of whatever’s around instead of sitting down for a whole meal.

A lot of it fits into the day anyway. At the shop, once things start running late, it’s easy to just keep working and not stop. There’s always another car, someone waiting, parts coming in, something that needs finishing. And then at home, with everybody moving around and the house being busy, I don’t really feel like making meals into some big thing. So I just go back to my own rules, I guess.

It feels more manageable that way. Like if I keep it to coffee, something small later, nothing complicated, then I’m not having to think about it too much or feel like I overdid it.
Do you ever make yourself exercise more or skip meals intentionally after you feel like you've eaten too much?

Yeah… I mean, I guess I do skip meals, but it doesn’t always feel like I’m doing it as some punishment or anything. It’s more like, if I feel like I ate more than I meant to, I go back to what feels controlled and simple.

Most days I’ll just have coffee in the morning, and then maybe later I’ll have a small sandwich, or honestly just half of whatever’s around. Especially at the shop, once the day gets going and we’re running late, it’s really easy to just keep working and not stop for a proper meal. There’s always another job or someone waiting on their car, so I’ll tell myself I’ll eat later, and then later turns into just grabbing something small.

And then when I get home, the house is busy and everybody’s doing their own thing, and I don’t really want to make a whole big thing out of food. So I kind of stick to my own rules — coffee, something small, keep it light. That feels better to me than sitting down and eating a full meal when I already feel like I might’ve overdone it.
After eating, do you ever make yourself vomit, take laxatives, or do anything else to try to get rid of the calories you’ve eaten?

No, not really. I mean… no, I don’t make myself throw up or anything like that. I’ve never been someone who could do that, and honestly the idea kind of bothers me.

Laxatives, no. I don’t mess with that stuff. I’m not saying my eating is perfectly normal or anything, but when I feel like I ate too much, it’s more that I try to keep things lighter afterward or get back to what feels manageable. I’m not trying to, like, physically get it out of me after I’ve eaten.

So… no vomiting, no laxatives. Nothing like that.

When you think about your weight or the way your body looks, do you see it differently than other people seem to? Like, do you feel like you're heavier or need to control it even when others don't see it that way?

Yeah… I think I probably do. I mean, people will say I look fine, or they’ll act like I’m making too much out of nothing, but it doesn’t feel like nothing to me.

If I get on the scale and it’s even up a pound, I notice it right away. Or if my jeans feel tighter — even just a little, like sitting in the truck or bending down at work — my head goes straight to, “Okay, you’re getting soft.” And I know maybe that sounds dramatic, but it really does bother me. I start thinking I’m going to feel heavier moving around cars at the shop, or slower getting up and down, crawling under things, being on my feet all day.

And I still play some ball when I can, so I think about that too. Like if I feel heavier, I picture myself being slower up and down the court, not moving the way I should. Other people might not see any difference at all, but I feel like I can tell. Or I convince myself I can tell. It makes me feel like I need to get it back under control before it turns into something more.
When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body, do you feel like certain parts of your body appear much larger or heavier than they actually are?

Yeah… I don’t know if I’d say I look in the mirror and see, like, one specific body part as huge or anything. It’s more the overall feeling that I’m getting bigger or softer than I should be.

Like, if the scale bumps up even one pound, I notice it. I know one pound probably shouldn’t matter that much, but in my head it does. Or if my jeans feel tighter, even just a little when I’m bending or sitting, I start thinking, “Okay, you’re getting soft.” And then it kind of sticks with me.

I think about work too — moving around cars, getting up and down, being on my feet all day — and I worry I’ll feel slower or heavier. Same with playing ball. If I feel like I’ve gained anything, I picture myself not moving as well up and down the court. So it’s not always that I can point to my stomach or legs or something and say, “That looks way bigger,” but I do feel like small changes mean I’m getting heavier, and I need to get it back under control.
Do you judge yourself mainly based on your weight or body shape?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t like saying that, but yeah, probably more than I should. It’s not like I’m walking around thinking, “My whole worth is a number,” exactly, but if the number changes, it can mess with my whole day.

Like if I step on the scale and it’s even up one pound, I notice it right away. I know that sounds ridiculous because a pound could be anything, but my brain doesn’t treat it that way. It goes straight to, “You’re getting soft,” or “You’re letting it slip.” Same thing if my jeans feel a little tighter when I’m bending down or sitting in the truck — then I start thinking about it over and over.

And it’s tied into how I see myself doing things, too. At work I’m moving around cars, getting up and down, on my feet, crawling around, and I start worrying I’m going to feel slower or heavier. Or when I play ball, I picture myself not moving as quick up and down the court. So yeah, my weight and how my body feels kind of becomes this measure of whether I’m doing okay or not. I know other people probably don’t see it that way, but in my head it feels really important.

And I still play some ball when I can, so I think about that too. Like if I feel heavier, I picture myself being slower up and down the court, not moving the way I should. Other people might not see any difference at all, but I feel like I can tell. Or I convince myself I can tell. It makes me feel like I need to get it back under control before it turns into something more.

The patient continues to endorse restrictive eating patterns driven by a fear of weight gain and body image concerns, supporting F50.0 (Anorexia Nervosa) and F50.8 (Other specified eating disorder).

doctor.question: When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body, do you feel like certain parts of your body appear much larger or heavier than they actually are?

patient.answer:
Yeah… I don’t know if I’d say I look in the mirror and see, like, one specific body part as huge or anything. It’s more the overall feeling that I’m getting bigger or softer than I should be.

Like, if the scale bumps up even one pound, I notice it. I know one pound probably shouldn’t matter that much, but in my head it does. Or if my jeans feel tighter, even just a little when I’m bending or sitting, I start thinking, “Okay, you’re getting soft.” And then it kind of sticks with me.

I think about work too — moving around cars, getting up and down, being on my feet all day — and I worry I’ll feel slower or heavier. Same with playing ball. If I feel like I’ve gained anything, I picture myself not moving as well up and down the court. So it’s not always that I can point to my stomach or legs or something and say, “That looks way bigger,” but I do feel like small changes mean I’m getting heavier, and I need to get it back under control.

inference.note: The patient continues to endorse restrictive eating behaviors, preoccupation with weight and body image, and a drive for thinness, particularly in the context of performance and physicality in work and sports. However, there is no evidence of compensatory behaviors such as vomiting or laxative misuse. The patient also exhibits body image disturbance, though it is more focused on perceived functional limitations rather than a distorted visual perception of specific body parts. doctor.question: Do you judge yourself mainly based on your weight or body shape?

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t like saying that, but yeah, probably more than I should. It’s not like I’m walking around thinking, “My whole worth is a number,” exactly, but if the number changes, it can mess with my whole day.

Like if I step on the scale and it’s even up one pound, I notice it right away. I know that sounds ridiculous because a pound could be anything, but my brain doesn’t treat it that way. It goes straight to, “You’re getting soft,” or “You’re letting it slip.” Same thing if my jeans feel a little tighter when I’m bending down or sitting in the truck — then I start thinking about it over and over.

And it’s tied into how I see myself doing things, too. At work I’m moving around cars, getting up and down, on my feet, crawling around, and I start worrying I’m going to feel slower or heavier. Or when I play ball, I picture myself not moving as quick up and down the court. So yeah, my weight and how my body feels kind of becomes this measure of whether I’m doing okay or not. I know other people probably don’t see it that way, but in my head it feels really important.
